summary: Vila Artemis is a browser game for young learners aged 7–13 that turns lunar mission planning into hands-on decisions. Guided by Dr. Bruna, a fictional science educator, players compare regions on a NASA LRO lunar map, build a shelter and communication antenna, manage power and life-support supplies, and protect their crew during a training solar storm. A second playable mission introduces polar ice research, individual crew assignments, equipment repairs, water extraction and data transmission. NASA LCROSS and M³ findings provide the polar science context, while recent NASA DONKI events influence an educational model of radio throughput. The game distinguishes NASA observations from authored rules: its resource units, exposure percentages, costs and mission times are teaching abstractions. Local saving and cached scientific resources support classroom use after an initial online visit. Our goal is to help learners explain why mission success depends on competing needs, rather than simply memorize space facts.
details:
WHAT WE BUILT

Vila Artemis is a playable 2D pixel-art lunar mission trainer for learners aged 7–13. The submitted web release is 0.2.3AH_age-of-NASA-LUNAR, revision submission-20261115. It combines a guided first expedition with a more open polar research mission. Dr. Bruna is a fictional science educator. This is an independent Space Apps project, with no claim of NASA endorsement or operational certification.

SUPPLEMENTARY GAMEPLAY VIDEO

YouTube gameplay recording - Vila Artemis Jogo: https://youtu.be/DPmZRBydbXY

Alternative 29-second hosted version: https://age-of-artemis-nasa.vercel.app/video/

This is an actual screen recording of the prototype with accelerated mission time and playback. SI-generated game art and AI-assisted code are visibly disclosed. The video is silent and shows the English interface. Our official Project Demonstration remains the seven-slide presentation linked above.

THE FIRST EXPEDITION

Players receive 100 fictional Lunar Coins and spend them on a Moon journey. A NASA LRO global color map introduces low- and high-latitude regions and their differences in water access, terrain and communications. The first mission uses the low-latitude option and water brought from Earth. Map markers are illustrative planning choices, not validated landing coordinates.

After a 12-second animated flight, players place a base and antenna on a 28-by-28 board while astronauts navigate around obstacles. Construction does not charge an upfront resource fee in the current missions; working increases energy use. Up to two astronauts can build together. The first data packet earns 20 knowledge points and normally takes 30 seconds to transmit.

An eight-second warning precedes a twelve-second training solar storm. Shelter reduces further exposure without erasing exposure already accumulated. Empty vital supplies or a full educational exposure budget ends the mission. A safe return awards 350 fictional coins and five additional knowledge points. Dialogue pauses the simulation so learners can read without losing supplies.

POLAR RESEARCH AND CREW DECISIONS

The second expedition costs 120 fictional coins and supports one to six astronauts. Solar panels and a water extractor cost 30 coins each. Players assign individual jobs: construction, research, extraction, repair or communication. Most tasks allow up to two workers; the radio uses one operator. A larger crew works faster but consumes more life-support supplies.

In a new polar mission, the crew researches 60 units of information, carries discoveries back to shelter, transmits them to Earth and returns safely. Water extraction supports survival but is not required for success. Equipment can malfunction and need repairs. Research becomes knowledge only when transmitted. A complete polar return awards 400 fictional coins and five extra knowledge points; partial and failed missions have separate outcomes.

NASA SCIENCE AND AUTHORED GAME RULES

The NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit supplies the global lunar appearance map. LCROSS findings from Cabeus and NASA M³ observations aboard ISRO's Chandrayaan-1 provide the evidence behind the polar ice lesson. The board is illustrative, not a georeferenced reconstruction of Cabeus.

NASA CCMC DONKI supplies archived notifications and recent FLR/SEP events. Recent event type, flare class and age influence an authored model of radio throughput. This illustrates a connection between solar activity and technology; it is not a measured lunar communications forecast. The scripted storm exercise is separate from real event arrival predictions. When recent data are unavailable, the game uses its documented training fallback.

The science panel presents historical ISS DosTel radiation readings from NASA OSDR RadLab in µGy/h and a published lunar radiation model from NASA NTRS 20240004047. ISS readings do not calibrate lunar biological risk or numerical shelter protection. Resource rates, exposure percentages, work times, equipment yields and currency are teaching abstractions. Source manifests include SHA-256 checksums for byte-integrity verification, not NASA certification.

BENEFIT, ACCESSIBILITY AND CREATIVITY

We connect regional planning, life support, shielding and research logistics in one decision loop: choose, build, protect, discover, transmit and return. The intended learning outcome is for children to explain trade-offs through consequences they have experienced. Learning gains have not yet been measured with children; classroom playtesting is a next step.

Portuguese, English and Spanish are available. The evaluation link opens in English. Progress is saved anonymously in the current browser, without names, passwords or cloud accounts. After a complete first visit over HTTPS, the application and local scientific resources are cached for offline use. Recent space-weather updates still require a network connection or a valid recent cache.

TECHNOLOGY AND VALIDATION

The web application uses TypeScript, Vite, Canvas 2D, CSS, Web Audio and a service worker. A Node.js server can serve the built app over a local network. Capacitor Android packaging exists in the project but is not the final web release being evaluated. Production build, ten simulation suites and browser journeys at desktop and mobile sizes were checked. These checks do not replace a child usability study or physical-device testing.

CURRENT LIMITS

Mars is a future destination and cannot be played. Greenhouse food production, dust maintenance, radiation-induced memory faults, optical laser communications and a Mars/MOXIE campaign are future ideas. The current game consumes food but has no playable greenhouse. It does not provide cross-device account synchronization, real NASA command transmission, certified astronaut training or a Play Store release. NASA Kilopower and CSA food-production materials are credited as future-work background only.

AI / SUPER INTELLIGENCE DISCLOSURE

The central idea originated with our human team. Google Antigravity helped organize the project, develop that concept and build the initial prototype. Google Gemini supported research, explanations and some artwork. ChatGPT (GPT-6 Astra) helped improve game-update logic. OpenAI Codex supported the final code review, automated validation, release adjustments, documentation and presentation. ChatGPT image generation adapted the fictional educator artwork. “Tob” is our name for an AI assistant, not a person. Visible SI artwork indicators, descriptive credits and machine-readable metadata document the assistance. Sound effects are synthesized by Web Audio through AI-assisted code; there is no generated spoken narrator. Scientific observations are attributed separately from authored rules.

TEAM

Reino da Ciência, Boa Vista, Brazil: Axl Oliveira Seabra, Jhonathan Hiroki Ybarra Hara, Maycon Douglas Alves Moraes and Bruna Sara de Brito Gomes. All four are registered team members.
